A.explanation: A smaller p.d. of $V/2$ would give a smaller power $P = V^2/R$, not the larger $20 \text{ W}$ observed.

B.explanation: New power is $20 \text{ W}$, which is $4$ times $5.0 \text{ W}$, so with $P = V^2/R$ the p.d. increases by $\sqrt{4} = 2$.

C.explanation: A p.d. of $3V$ would give $9$ times the power, $45 \text{ W}$, which is larger than the $20 \text{ W}$ calculated from $45.0 \text{ J}$ in $2.25 \text{ s}$.

D.explanation: A p.d. of $4V$ would give $16$ times the power, $80 \text{ W}$, which confuses the factor $4$ in power with the factor in p.d.

hints: First use the $45.0 \text{ J}$ transferred in $2.25 \text{ s}$ to find the new power dissipated in the resistor.
For a fixed resistor $R$, use $P = V^2/R$ so power is proportional to the square of the p.d.
Compare the new power with the original $5.0 \text{ W}$ and take the square root of the power ratio to get the p.d. ratio.
walkthrough: Calculate the new power from energy and time: $P_{new} = E/t = 45.0/2.25 = 20 \text{ W}$.
Recall for a fixed resistance that $P = V^2/R$, so $P$ is proportional to $V^2$ because $R$ is unchanged.
